title: Does Baseball Still Need Divisions To Matter This Much?
contentHtml:
As I wrote in Scoreboard yesterday, this final week of the MLB season still has a lot of outstanding items to resolve — including both seeding battles, wild-cards and even a few remaining division races.

Subscribe now

But what exactly do we make of those divisions? While the winners of the AL Central (Guardians or White Sox?) and AL West (Rangers or Astros?) are not yet known, we do know that both divisions will be won with records that rank among the worst ever. According to my Elo forecast simulations on Tuesday afternoon, the average winner of the Central (across 50,000 simulations) finished the regular season with 84.3 wins, while the average West champ won just 81.4 games on average:

For context, the worst division champ by winning percentage in a season1 since the concept was first introduced in 1969 were the 2005 NL West champion San Diego Padres, with a record of 82-80. Based on the chart above, there was on Tuesday an 85 percent chance the AL West winner would at least tie that anti-record, a 54 percent they would break it to become the first .500 (or worse) division winner in MLB history, and a 20 percent chance of being won with an outright losing record. (The AL Central winner also had a small chance — 3 percent — of tying the record at 82 wins.)
